title: Type the text columns of an imported CSV
prompt: Mosaic's Import CSV stores every column as text. Turn raw_orders into typed columns: order_id as INTEGER; amount as DOUBLE, or NULL when it is blank or not a number; status trimmed and lower-cased, or NULL when blank. Keep every row.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: raw_orders(order_id VARCHAR, amount VARCHAR, status VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: order_id, amount, status. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: CAST fails the whole query on one bad value; TRY_CAST returns NULL instead. An empty string is not NULL, and ' Shipped' is not 'shipped'.

starter_source:
SELECT order_id, amount, status
FROM raw_orders

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: TRY_CAST(x AS DOUBLE) returns NULL instead of raising an error.
NULLIF(value, '') turns an empty string into NULL.
explanation: Imported text needs explicit, forgiving typing: TRY_CAST for numbers, TRIM/LOWER to normalise categories and NULLIF so blanks become real NULLs that aggregates ignore.
follow_ups: How would you count the rows whose amount failed to parse?
When should a bad value stop the pipeline instead of becoming NULL?

title: Keep the latest change per key from a CDC feed
prompt: customer_changes is a change feed. Return the current row per customer: the change with the latest updated_at; when two changes share updated_at, the one with the higher ingest_seq wins. Output customer_id, email, updated_at.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: customer_changes(customer_id INTEGER, email VARCHAR, updated_at TIMESTAMP, ingest_seq INTEGER)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, email, updated_at. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Joining back on MAX(updated_at) or filtering RANK() = 1 returns two rows when timestamps tie; ordering by ingest_seq alone picks late-arriving old data.

starter_source:
SELECT customer_id, email, updated_at
FROM customer_changes

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: ROW_NUMBER() gives exactly one row number 1 per partition, even on ties.
Order by the business timestamp first, then by the tie-breaker.
explanation: Deduplicating a change feed needs a total order per key: the business timestamp decides, and a deterministic tie-breaker (ingest sequence) resolves equal timestamps. QUALIFY filters on the window result directly.
follow_ups: What if the feed also contains deletes?
Why is ingest order alone unsafe with late-arriving data?

title: Find customers without orders when keys can be NULL
prompt: Return the customers who never placed an order. Guest checkouts store orders.customer_id as NULL. Output customer_id, name.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: customers(customer_id INTEGER, name VARCHAR); orders(order_id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, name. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: x NOT IN (subquery) is never true once the subquery contains a NULL, so one guest order silently empties the result.

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: NOT EXISTS compares row by row and is not affected by NULLs elsewhere.
Try the NOT IN version on the guest-order case and compare.
explanation: NOT IN expands to a chain of <> comparisons; any comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole predicate is never true. NOT EXISTS (or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) is the NULL-safe anti-join.
follow_ups: Rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN anti-join.
Which other operators behave surprisingly with NULLs?

title: Turn login days into streaks (gaps and islands)
prompt: A user can log in several times a day. For each user, return every streak of consecutive calendar days with at least one login: user_id, streak_start, streak_end (DATEs) and days (the streak length).

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: logins(user_id INTEGER, login_at TIMESTAMP)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: user_id, streak_start, streak_end, days. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Numbering raw logins instead of distinct days breaks a streak whenever someone logs in twice a day; numbering without PARTITION BY user_id mixes users.

starter_source:
SELECT user_id, CAST(login_at AS DATE) AS streak_start, CAST(login_at AS DATE) AS streak_end, 1 AS days
FROM logins

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Reduce to one row per user and day first.
Consecutive days minus their row number give the same constant: group by it.
explanation: In an island of consecutive days, day - row_number() is constant, so it identifies the island. Deduplicating to days first and partitioning by user are both essential.
follow_ups: Return only each user's longest streak.
How would you allow one missed day inside a streak?

title: Sessionize clicks with a 30-minute inactivity gap
prompt: A new session starts at a user's first click and whenever more than 30 minutes passed since that user's previous click (exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session). Return user_id, session_no (1, 2, ... per user), session_start, session_end and events.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: clicks(user_id INTEGER, event_at TIMESTAMP)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: user_id, session_no, session_start, session_end, events. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Using >= splits sessions at exactly 30 minutes; LAG without PARTITION BY user_id compares one user's click with another user's.

starter_source:
SELECT user_id, 1 AS session_no, MIN(event_at) AS session_start, MAX(event_at) AS session_end, COUNT(*) AS events
FROM clicks
GROUP BY user_id

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: LAG(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) gives the previous click.
A running SUM of 'starts a session' flags numbers the sessions.
explanation: Flag each click that opens a session (first click, or gap over the threshold), then a running sum of the flags is the session number. The boundary condition (> vs >=) is part of the business definition.
follow_ups: Add a session duration in minutes.
How would a maximum session length of 4 hours change the query?

title: Price each trade with the last quote before it (ASOF join)
prompt: For every trade, attach the latest price of the same symbol quoted at or before traded_at. Trades with no earlier quote keep price NULL. Output trade_id, symbol, traded_at, price.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: trades(trade_id INTEGER, symbol VARCHAR, traded_at TIMESTAMP); prices(symbol VARCHAR, quoted_at TIMESTAMP, price DOUBLE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: trade_id, symbol, traded_at, price. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: An inner ASOF JOIN drops trades that happened before the first quote; a strict > misses a quote at exactly the trade time.

starter_source:
SELECT t.trade_id, t.symbol, t.traded_at, NULL::DOUBLE AS price
FROM trades AS t

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: DuckDB's ASOF JOIN matches the nearest row satisfying the inequality.
Use ASOF LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched trades.
explanation: An as-of join picks, per left row, the closest right row that satisfies one inequality, after equality keys. It replaces a correlated MAX() subquery or a window over a union.
follow_ups: Write the same query without ASOF using a correlated subquery.
How would you reject quotes older than 5 minutes?

title: Build SCD type 2 validity ranges from a change log
prompt: tier_changes lists each tier a customer moved to and the day it happened. Build the SCD2 history: customer_id, tier, valid_from (the change day), valid_to (the next change day for that customer, NULL for the current row) and is_current.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: tier_changes(customer_id INTEGER, tier VARCHAR, changed_on DATE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: customer_id, tier, valid_from, valid_to, is_current. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: LEAD without PARTITION BY customer_id hands one customer's next change to another customer.

starter_source:
SELECT customer_id, tier, changed_on AS valid_from, NULL::DATE AS valid_to, TRUE AS is_current
FROM tier_changes

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: LEAD(changed_on) looks at the next change.
The current version is the one with no next change.
explanation: SCD2 ranges come from the next change per key: valid_to = LEAD(changed_on) within the customer. Keeping valid_to exclusive (the next start) avoids off-by-one gaps.
follow_ups: Find the tier a customer had on 2026-05-01.
How would you collapse consecutive rows with the same tier?

title: Compute the table after an upsert (MERGE) batch
prompt: Apply the updates batch to target as a full-row upsert: an update replaces the whole target row with the same id (including NULLs it carries), target rows without an update stay unchanged, and new ids are inserted. ids are unique in each table. Return the resulting rows: id, name, city.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: target(id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, city VARCHAR); updates(id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, city VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: id, name, city. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: COALESCE(u.city, t.city) keeps the old value when the update deliberately clears a column; a LEFT JOIN from target drops inserts.

starter_source:
SELECT id, name, city
FROM target

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Every update row ends up in the result as is.
Keep only target rows whose id is not in the batch.
explanation: A full-row upsert is 'all incoming rows' plus 'untouched existing rows'. Column-wise COALESCE implements a partial update, which is a different contract.
follow_ups: How would a partial update (only non-NULL columns) differ?
Add a deletes batch to the same result.

title: List every data-quality rule each order breaks
prompt: Check each order against three rules for the batch dated 2026-09-30: missing_email (NULL or blank), negative_amount (amount below 0; zero is allowed) and future_date (order_date after 2026-09-30). Return one row per broken rule: order_id, rule.

prompt: Report revenue for every month from January to June 2026, including months without sales (revenue 0). Ignore sales outside that range. Output month (the first day of the month, as a DATE) and revenue.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: sales(sold_on DATE, amount DOUBLE)

sections.title: Common pitfall

title: Measure a view → cart → purchase funnel
prompt: events has one row per user action (view, cart, purchase), with repeats. A user counts at a step only if they also did every earlier step. Return step, users and pct_of_viewers (users / viewers * 100, rounded to 1 decimal; NULL when there are no viewers).

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: events(user_id INTEGER, step VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: step, users, pct_of_viewers. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: Counting events instead of distinct users inflates every step; counting buyers who never added to cart overstates conversion.

starter_source:
SELECT step, COUNT(*) AS users, NULL::DOUBLE AS pct_of_viewers
FROM events
GROUP BY step

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: Collapse to one row per user with BOOL_OR flags first.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) counts the users at each step.
explanation: Funnels are user-level: reduce events to per-user step flags, then require the earlier flags for each later step. NULLIF guards the division when nobody viewed.
follow_ups: Require the steps to happen in time order.
Split the funnel by acquisition channel.

title: Median delivery time per carrier
prompt: Return each carrier's median delivery time in days: carrier, median_days (a DOUBLE; with an even count, the mean of the two middle values).

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: deliveries(carrier VARCHAR, days INTEGER)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: carrier, median_days. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: AVG is pulled by one lost parcel; quantile_disc(0.5) returns an existing value instead of interpolating an even count.

FROM deliveries
GROUP BY carrier

title: Monthly cohort retention counts
prompt: A customer's cohort is the month of their first order. For each cohort and each month_offset (0 = the cohort month, 1 = the next month, ...), count the distinct customers who ordered in that month. Output cohort_month (DATE, first day of month), month_offset (INTEGER), customers. Only list offsets with activity.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: orders(customer_id INTEGER, ordered_on DATE)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: cohort_month, month_offset, customers. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: COUNT(*) counts orders, not customers; deriving the cohort from each order's own month puts every order at offset 0.

starter_source:
SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', ordered_on) AS DATE) AS cohort_month, 0 AS month_offset, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: First find each customer's first order month.
date_diff('month', a, b) counts month boundaries between two dates.
explanation: Cohort tables fix each customer's starting month once, then measure later activity relative to it. Distinct customers, not orders, make retention comparable across cohorts.
follow_ups: Turn the counts into retention percentages of the offset-0 size.
Pivot offsets 0-3 into columns.

title: Select the next incremental batch with a watermark
prompt: watermark stores, per source table, the last updated_at already loaded. Return the source_rows rows to load next for table 'source_rows': updated_at strictly after its watermark, or every row on the first run (no watermark row). Output id, updated_at.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: source_rows(id INTEGER, updated_at TIMESTAMP); watermark(table_name VARCHAR, last_loaded_at TIMESTAMP)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: id, updated_at. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: >= reloads the boundary row every run; comparing with a NULL watermark returns nothing on the first run; forgetting table_name uses another table's watermark.

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: A scalar subquery can read the watermark.
COALESCE gives the first run a very old default watermark.
explanation: Incremental loads are only correct with a strict > comparison against the table's own watermark and an explicit first-run default; after loading, the watermark advances to the batch's MAX(updated_at).
follow_ups: What goes wrong if two rows share the watermark timestamp but only one was loaded?
Compute the new watermark value for this batch.

title: Pivot ticket statuses with COUNT FILTER
prompt: For each opened_on day, return open_count, closed_count and total tickets. Status values are exactly 'open' or 'closed'.

sections.title: Tables
sections.body: tickets(opened_on DATE, status VARCHAR)

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Columns in this order: opened_on, open_count, closed_count, total. Row order does not matter.

sections.title: Common pitfall
sections.body: COUNT(status = 'open') counts every non-NULL boolean, FALSE included, so it equals the total.

starter_source:
SELECT opened_on, 0 AS open_count, 0 AS closed_count, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM tickets
GROUP BY opened_on

visible_checks.description: Public example: the tables shown in data_context.

hints: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE condition) counts only matching rows.
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) is the portable equivalent.
explanation: FILTER makes conditional counts explicit. COUNT(expr) counts non-NULL values, and a FALSE boolean is not NULL, which is the classic trap.
follow_ups: Add the share of closed tickets per day.
Pivot per week instead of per day.
